{{Short description|Mathematical theorem relating to limits}}
{{distinguish|Heine–Borel theorem}}
<!--==== Sequences and nets {{anchor|Heine definition of continuity}}====-->

'''Heine's theorem''', named after the German mathematician [[Eduard Heine]], establishes a link in [[mathematical analysis]] between [[Limit of a function|limits of functions]] and [[Limit of a sequence|limits of sequences]]. The theorem states that the existence and value of the limit of a function at a point can be characterized by the limits of all sequences that converge to that point. Conversely, information about sequential limits can be used to determine function limits. As a consequence, many properties of limits of functions may be derived from the corresponding properties of limits of sequences.<ref>{{cite book
|title=Mathematical Analysis
|edition=6th
|volume=1
|first1=Vladimir Antonovich
|last1=Zorich
|series=Universitext
|publisher=Springer
|location=Burlington, Vermont, USA
|year=2015
|isbn=978-3-662-48790-7
|doi=10.1007/978-3-662-48792-1
|page=110
|language=en}}</ref>

Specifically, it contains a statement with two parts:

'''Forward statement:''' Let <math>f</math> be a function and let <math>a</math> be an accumulation point of its domain. If <math display="block">\lim\limits_{x\to a}f\left(x\right)=L,</math> then for every sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> that converges to <math>a</math> and satisfies <math>x_n\ne a</math> for all <math>n</math>, the sequence <math>\left\{f\left(x_n\right)\right\}</math> converges to <math>L</math>; that is, <math display="block">\lim\limits_{x\to a}f\left(x\right)=L\implies\forall\left\{x_n\right\}\left(\left(x_n\to a\land x_n\ne a\right)\implies f\left(x_n\right)\to L\right).</math>

'''Converse statement:''' Conversely, if for every sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> with <math>x_n \to a</math> and <math>x_n \neq a</math> for all <math>n</math>, the sequence <math>\left\{f(x_n)\right\}</math> converges to the same limit <math>L</math>, then the limit of <math>f</math> at <math>a</math> exists and equals <math>L</math>; in symbols,
<math display="block">\forall\left\{x_n\right\}\left(\left(x_n\to a\land x_n\ne a\right)\implies f\left(x_n\right)\to L\right)\implies\lim\limits_{x\to a}f\left(x\right)=L.</math>

==Background==
In several contexts, the topology of a space is conveniently specified in terms of [[limit points]]. This is often accomplished by specifying when a point is the [[limit of a sequence]]. Still, for some spaces that are too large in some sense, one specifies also when a point is the limit of more general sets of points [[Indexed family|indexed]] by a [[directed set]], known as [[Net (mathematics)|nets]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=E. H. |last2=Smith |first2=H. L. |year=1922 |title=A General Theory of Limits |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=102–121 |doi=10.2307/2370388 |jstor=2370388 }}</ref> A function is (Heine-)continuous only if it takes limits of sequences to limits of sequences. In the former case, preservation of limits is also sufficient; in the latter, a function may preserve all limits of sequences yet still fail to be continuous, and preservation of nets is a necessary and sufficient condition.

In detail, a function <math>f:X\to Y</math> is '''[[Sequential space|sequentially continuous]]''' if whenever a sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> in <math>X</math> converges to a limit <math>x,</math> the sequence <math>\left\{f\left(x_n\right)\right\}</math> converges to <math>f\left(x\right).</math>  Thus, sequentially continuous functions "preserve sequential limits."  Every continuous function is sequentially continuous.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baron |first1=S. |last2=Leader |first2=Solomon |date=1966 |title=Solution to Problem #5299 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2314834 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=73 |issue=6 |pages=677–678 |doi=10.2307/2314834 |jstor=2314834 |issn=0002-9890|url-access=subscription }}</ref> If <math>X</math> is a [[first-countable space]] and [[Axiom of countable choice|countable choice]] holds, then the converse also holds: any function preserving sequential limits is continuous. In particular, if <math>X</math> is a metric space, sequential continuity and continuity are equivalent. For non-first-countable spaces, sequential continuity might be strictly weaker than continuity. (The spaces for which the two properties are equivalent are called [[sequential space]]s.)<ref>{{Cite web |last1=math |last2=Sleziak |first2=Martin |date=Dec 6, 2016 |title=Example of different topologies with same convergent sequences |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/76691/example-of-different-topologies-with-same-convergent-sequences |access-date=2022-06-27 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |publisher=StackOverflow |language=en}}</ref> <!-- Note that the creator of this StackOverflow page is a math professor. As per [[WP:BLOG]], a self-published source like this one can be reliable as long as the author has relevant expertise. --> This motivates the consideration of nets instead of sequences in general topological spaces. Continuous functions preserve the limits of nets, and this property characterizes continuous functions.

==Formal statement==

Consider the case of real-valued functions of one real variable:<ref>{{cite book |title=Calculus and Analysis in Euclidean Space |edition=illustrated |first1=Jerry |last1=Shurman |series=Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics |publisher=Springer |year=2016 |isbn=978-3-319-49314-5 |pages=271–272 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-49314-5 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-49314-5|language=en}}</ref>

{{math theorem|name=Theorem|note=|style=|math_statement=A function <math>f : A \subseteq \R \to \R</math> is continuous at <math>x_0</math> if and only if it is [[sequentially continuous]] at that point.}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=('''Sufficiency''') Assume that <math>f:A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is [[Limit_of_a_function#epsilon-delta definition|continuous]] at <math>x_0</math> (in the sense of <math>\varepsilon-\delta</math> continuity). Let <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> be a sequence converging at <math>x_0</math> (such a sequence always exists, for example, <math>x_n=x_0</math> for all <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math><ref>Here <math>\mathbb{N}</math> and the term "natural number" follow the British convention, referring to positive integers. The same applies hereafter. --- Noted by editor</ref>). Since <math>f</math> is continuous at <math>x_0</math>, then <math display=block>\forall\varepsilon>0\exists\delta>0\forall x\left(0<\left|x-x_0\right|<\delta\implies\left|f\left(x\right)-f\left(x_0\right)\right|<\varepsilon\right).\quad (*)</math> For any <math>\delta</math> that satisfies conditions above, one can always find a natural number <math>\nu</math> such that for arbitrary <math>n>\nu</math>, <math display=block>\left|x_n-x_0\right|<\delta.</math> holds, since <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> converges at <math>x_0</math>. Combining this with expression <math>(*)</math>, then <math display=block>\forall\varepsilon>0\exists\nu\in\mathbb{N}\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\left(n>\nu\implies\left|f\left(x_n\right)-f\left(x_0\right)\right|<\varepsilon\right).</math> According to the definition of limit of a sequence, the expression above equivalents to <math>\left\{f\left(x_n\right)\right\}</math>, id est <math>f</math> is sequentially continuous at <math>x_0</math>.

('''Necessity''') Assume that <math>f</math> is sequentially continuous, and <math>f</math> is not continuous at <math>x_0</math>, namely <math display=block>\exists\varepsilon>0\forall\delta>0\exists x\left(0<\left|x-x_0\right|<\delta\land\left|f\left(x\right)-f\left(x_0\right)\right|\ge\varepsilon\right).</math> Then one can take <math>\delta=\frac{1}{n}</math>, where <math>n</math> is an arbitrary natural number, and call the corresponding point <math>x_n:=x</math>. In this way we have defined a sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> such that <math display=block>\exists\varepsilon>0\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\left(\left|x_n-x_0\right|<\frac{1}{n}\land\left|f\left(x_n\right)-f\left(x_0\right)\right|\ge\varepsilon\right).</math> By the construction above, <math>f\left(x_n\right)\to f\left(x_0\right)</math> is false when <math>x_n\to x_0</math>, which contradicts the hypothesis of sequential continuity. Hence the proposition "If <math>f</math> is sequentially continuous at <math>x_0</math>, then <math>f</math> is continuous at <math>x_0</math>" holds.

<math>\blacksquare</math>}}
